paraphrase: 'Atha' (now) means 'after' the acquisition of the fourfold means: discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal, dispassion toward enjoyments here and hereafter, the wealth of calm, self-control and the rest, and the longing for liberation — not after the inquiry into ritual duty (dharma).

tags.stage_native: mumukṣu endowed with the four means

paraphrase: The existence of Brahman is known because it is the self of all: everyone is aware that he exists and never thinks 'I am not'; but because there are conflicting views about what the self is, inquiry is needed.

Brahman is known in two forms: as qualified by limiting adjuncts — the distinctions of name and form and their modifications — and as the opposite of that, free of all adjuncts; thousands of Upaniṣadic texts show this twofoldness according as knowledge or ignorance is in view. In the state of ignorance all usage, including that of worshipper and worshipped, applies to Brahman: some meditations on Brahman qualified by attributes are for prosperity, some for gradual liberation, some for the success of rites, and their fruits differ with the attributes meditated on, though the Lord meditated on is one. Thus the one Brahman is taught in the Vedānta both as related to adjuncts, as the object of worship, and as free of adjuncts, as the object of knowledge.

original.text: dvirūpaṃ hi brahmāvagamyate, nāmarūpavikārabhedopādhiviśiṣṭaṃ, tadviparītaṃ ca sarvopādhivivarjitam /
original.licence: GRETIL — quotation for reference with attribution

speaker: Śaṅkara
notes: Also verified: 'evamekamapi brahmāpekṣitopādhisaṃbandhaṃ nirastopādhisaṃbandhaṃ copāsyatvena jñeyatvena ca vedānteṣūpadiśyata'.

paraphrase: After commenting on the sūtras as though the 'one consisting of bliss' were Brahman, Śaṅkara argues that it is a sheath (kośa) and that the sūtras rather refer to 'Brahman, the tail, the support' (TU 2.5): the suffix -maya denotes modification, and the bliss-sheath has parts (joy, delight) and is not the highest.

Knowledge of an existing thing depends on the thing itself (vastu-tantra), not on the person's choice (puruṣa-tantra) as action does; knowledge of Brahman therefore depends on the thing, and inference serves only in support of the Upaniṣadic texts.

The great scripture beginning with the Ṛgveda — enlarged by many branches of learning, illumining all things like a lamp, almost omniscient — has Brahman as its source (yoni): such a scripture could arise from none but the omniscient; it issued from that great being without effort, as breath ('the Ṛgveda is the out-breathing of this great being'). Or, alternatively: that scripture is the source, i.e. the means of knowledge, of Brahman — Brahman as the cause of the world's origin is known from scripture alone.

original.text: mahata ṛgvedādeḥ śāstrasyānekavidyāsthānopabṛṃhitasya pradīpavatsarvārthāvadyotinaḥ sarvajñakalpasya yoniḥ kāraṇaṃbrahma /

speaker: Śaṅkara

paraphrase: Liberation is not something to be produced, reached, modified or purified by action; it is eternal bodilessness, the very nature of Brahman. Hence Brahman-knowledge is not subordinate to injunctions, and the Upaniṣads are authoritative in themselves for an existent reality, not merely as adjuncts to ritual.
notes: Summary of a long passage (the samanvaya section); recorded here as the Vedānta side of the siddha/sādhya dispute.

paraphrase: Quoted verses: once the self as the existent Brahman is known, the secondary and false selves (son, body) being negated, how could there be anything to be done? The self is a knower only until the self to be sought is known; once known, it is free from knower-hood, evil and defects.
notes: Three verses introduced 'api cāhuḥ'; later commentators ascribe them to Sundarapāṇḍya (low confidence).

paraphrase: Śaṅkara accepts that the world is preceded by the Vedic word (words as eternal universals from which the individuals are produced), but rejects the sphoṭa: 'the letters alone are the word', says the revered Upavarṣa; the letters, apprehended one by one and gathered in a single cognition with the last, convey the meaning, and an imperceptible sphoṭa is needlessly assumed.
notes: The quotation 'varṇā eva tu śabda iti bhagavān upavarṣaḥ' is well known; the rest paraphrases the bhāṣya's argument from memory.

paraphrase: The eternity of the Veda has already been established from the fact that no independent author of it is remembered; since the world with its fixed forms — the gods and the rest — arises from the Vedic word, the Vedic word must also be understood to be eternal. A mantra says the sacrificers 'found the speech that had entered the seers', i.e. speech already existing; and Vyāsa's smṛti says that at the beginning the great seers, permitted by the Self-born, obtained through austerity the Vedas with the histories that had disappeared at the end of the age.

original.licence: GRETIL — quotation for reference with attribution

speaker: Śaṅkara

paraphrase: Śūdras are not eligible for Vedic study, but those like Vidura and Dharmavyādha attained knowledge through tendencies from former lives; the fruit of knowledge cannot be denied to them, and the Itihāsas and Purāṇas may be taught to all four classes.

Of the three teachers' views, Kāśakṛtsna's — that the supreme Lord himself exists as the individual self — accords with scripture; the difference between jīva and Brahman is due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of name and form produced by ignorance.

Brahman is both the material cause (like clay for pots) and the efficient cause (like the potter), since scripture promises that by knowing it everything is known and gives the illustration of clay and its products; there is no other overseer.

The effect (the world) is non-different from its cause (Brahman), a mere name dependent on speech, as pots are clay; all worldly and Vedic dealings are valid until the knowledge of the self as Brahman, as dream dealings are until waking; the Lord's lordship, omniscience and omnipotence depend on the limiting adjuncts of name and form produced by ignorance.

The Lord creates without any purpose of his own, as a king at leisure plays or as breathing goes on by itself; and scripture's account of creation is concerned only with the empirical realm of name and form produced by ignorance, its aim being to teach that Brahman is the self.
The Lord is like rain (parjanya), the common cause of all plants, whose varieties depend on their own seeds: inequality among beings depends on their own merit and demerit.

The Buddhist who holds that everything is momentary must hold that the perceiver too is momentary; but that is impossible because of memory. Remembering follows an experience and is possible only when the one who experienced and the one who remembers are one agent: everyone has the direct recognition 'I saw that, and now I see this'; if the agents were different one would think 'I remember, another saw'. Even the momentarist takes himself as the one agent of seeing and remembering, and recognizes his cognitions from birth to his last breath as his own. Nor can the unity be explained by similarity, for grasping that one moment is similar to another requires a single grasper of both moments, which the momentarist cannot admit.

original.text: apica darśanasmaraṇayoḥ kartaryekasminpratyakṣaḥ pratyabhijñāpratyayaḥ sarvasya lokasya prasiddho 'hamado 'drākṣamidaṃ paśyāmīti /

speaker: Śaṅkara

paraphrase: Against the Buddhist who holds that there is only consciousness (vijñānavāda): the non-existence of external objects cannot be established, because they are perceived — in every cognition an external thing, a pillar, a wall, a pot, a cloth, is apprehended. One who perceives an object through contact of the senses and says 'I do not perceive it and it does not exist' is like one who eats, feels satisfied and says he neither eats nor is satisfied. Even those who deny the external object say that the inner cognizable appears 'as if external', which presupposes the external. The self-established witness (sākṣin) of cognition cannot be denied; and this is not the Buddhist's own self-luminous cognition in other words, since cognition is admitted to arise, perish and be many.

original.text: na khalvabhāvo bāhyasyārthasyādhyavasātuṃ śakyate / kasmāt / upalabdheḥ / upalabhyate hi pratipratyayaṃ bāhyo'rthaḥ stambhaḥ kuḍyaṃ ghaṭaḥ paṭa iti /
original.licence: GRETIL — quotation for reference with attribution

speaker: Śaṅkara
notes: Also: 'svayaṃsiddhasya ca sākṣiṇo 'pratyākhyeyatvāt' (same section, verified in the same file).

paraphrase: The store-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) posited as the seat of latent impressions cannot be their locus, since it too is admitted to be momentary: without one enduring, connected knower, or an unchanging seer of all objects, the deposit of impressions, memory and recognition are impossible. Having refuted both Buddhist positions — that of external objects and that of consciousness only — Śaṅkara says that no effort is made to refute the doctrine of the void (śūnyavāda), since it is opposed by every means of knowledge: worldly usage, established by all the means of knowledge, cannot be denied without knowing another reality.

speaker: Śaṅkara
notes: In the GRETIL numbering sūtra 2.2.31 is 'kṣaṇikatvāc ca'; some editions number the sūtras of this section differently.

paraphrase: Having refuted the realist, idealist and void doctrines, Śaṅkara says the Buddha, by teaching three mutually incompatible doctrines, showed either incoherence or hostility toward beings, and that the Buddhist teaching is to be disregarded by those who seek the good.

The view that the Lord is only the efficient cause, the ruler but not the material cause, opposes the Vedānta's unity of Brahman and takes many non-Vedic forms: some following Sāṃkhya-Yoga; the Māheśvaras hold that five categories - effect, cause, union, rule and end of suffering - were taught by the Lord Paśupati for release from the bond of the paśus, and that Paśupati is the efficient cause. This is inconsistent: a Lord who makes beings low, middle and high would have passion and aversion like us; if he acts in dependence on beings' karma, karma and Lord would depend on each other; beginninglessness does not remove this, as with a chain of the blind.

paraphrase: Śaṅkara reports the Bhāgavata teaching: Vāsudeva, the highest Self, abides divided fourfold as Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa (the individual soul), Pradyumna (mind) and Aniruddha (ego-sense), and is to be approached by going to the temple, gathering materials, worship, study and yoga. He accepts the worship and meditation of Vāsudeva as not contrary to scripture, but rejects the origination of the soul (Saṅkarṣaṇa) from Vāsudeva, since an originated soul would be impermanent and could not attain liberation; he also finds contradiction and opposition to the Veda in the system, citing its account that Śāṇḍilya learned this śāstra after not finding the highest good in the four Vedas.
speaker: Śaṅkara
notes: The Pāñcarātra doctrine here is reported by its critic. Paraphrase from memory; not checked against a local e-text. The five practices named correspond to the Pāñcarātra's five daily periods.

paraphrase: The Pāñcarātra's worship of Vāsudeva, its practices of approach, offering, study and meditation, and its devotion are not refuted; what is refuted is the doctrine that the individual self (Saṅkarṣaṇa) and the mind originate from Vāsudeva.
notes: Placed at the section 2.2.42–45; exact sūtra of this remark uncertain.

paraphrase: The jīva is to be understood as a reflection (ābhāsa) of the supreme self, like the sun reflected in water; as the trembling of one reflection does not affect others, the karma of one jīva does not pass to another.
Brahman appears as if sharing the defects and differences of its adjuncts, as the sun's reflection seems to increase, decrease and tremble with the water; in itself it is untouched.

'Not so, not so' negates the two forms (gross and subtle, formed and formless) of Brahman already mentioned, not Brahman itself, which the text then names 'the reality of the real'; negation must end in something not negated.

Śaṅkara says that the proof of the self's existence, drawn from this Brahma Sūtra passage, was given by Śabara in the section on the means of knowledge, and that the revered Upavarṣa, when the occasion arose in the first treatise (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā), deferred it saying 'we shall explain it in the Śārīraka'.
notes: Wording checked in a local Advaita commentary e-text; sūtra number per Śaṅkara's recension (some editions 3.3.54).

paraphrase: Some Lokāyatikas, who see the self in the body alone and deny a self apart from it, hold that although consciousness is not seen in earth and the other external elements, singly or together, it may arise in them when transformed into the shape of a body; they say 'from them, consciousness', 'cognition is like intoxicating power', 'the person is the body qualified by consciousness'; there is no self apart from the body able to go to heaven or to liberation; their reason: (consciousness) exists where the body exists — what exists when something exists and not otherwise is its property, as heat and light are of fire.

original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted read-only for reference

notes: Reported by an opponent: Śaṅkara (Advaita), stating the pūrvapakṣa. Checked in the local e-text.

paraphrase: Rather the self is distinct from the body, because consciousness does not exist whenever the body exists: breath, movement, consciousness and memory are absent in the dead body though form and colour remain, and the body's qualities are perceived by others while consciousness and memory are not; and the Lokāyatika must be asked what this consciousness is — it is the experiencing of the elements, and what experiences the elements cannot be one of them.
speaker: Śaṅkara
notes: Checked in the local e-text (sūtra 'vyatirekas tadbhāvābhāvitvān na tūpalabdhivat').

paraphrase: Works such as sacrifice are needed not for the fruit of knowledge (liberation) but for the arising of knowledge, as a horse is used for drawing a chariot, not for ploughing; once knowledge has arisen they are not needed for liberation.
The knower of Brahman is untouched by future sins and his past sins are destroyed, because he realizes himself as the non-agent Brahman; this is the state of liberation while living.

Works that have already begun their effect (prārabdha) are not destroyed by knowledge but continue until exhausted, just as a potter's wheel keeps turning for a while after the push that set it going has ceased; for one who has knowledge, the body continues till death.
notes: The potter's-wheel illustration is placed here from memory (moderate confidence); a released arrow is used in the same sense elsewhere in the tradition.

paraphrase: Repetition of the teaching is for one who does not realize at the first hearing; for one who understands 'tat tvam asi' at once, repetition is useless. Repetition removes the obstacles of doubt and contrary notions.
The prāṇas of the knower of the attributeless Brahman do not depart: being Brahman, he merges here; the path of the gods is for those who meditated on the qualified Brahman.

Those who meditated on the qualified Brahman go by the path of light to the Brahma-world and are liberated with Hiraṇyagarbha at the end of the cycle (gradual liberation, krama-mukti); the knower of the attributeless Brahman is liberated at once.

paraphrase: Subject and object — the 'you' and the 'I' — are opposed like darkness and light, so neither can be the other; yet, failing to discriminate them, people superimpose each and its attributes on the other and say 'I am this, this is mine'. This natural, beginningless superimposition, a wrong cognition, is the root of all empirical dealings.
notes: Opening of the adhyāsa-bhāṣya (upodghāta, the introduction before 1.1.1); the original gives only the first clause.

original.edition: vulgate wording recalled from memory (verify against an edition)

paraphrase: Superimposition is the appearance, of the nature of memory, of something previously seen, in something else.

paraphrase: The learned call this superimposition, so defined, ignorance (avidyā), and the ascertainment of the real by discriminating it they call knowledge (vidyā).

All the means of knowledge — perception and the rest — and all scriptures dealing with injunctions, prohibitions and liberation, have as their sphere the one who is under ignorance, since without identifying with body and senses one could not be a knower, agent or enjoyer.
